So I had a chance meeting recently with a very senior IT leader at one of the world’s largest companies.
A few months back, they’d decided on their new CRM and other business process app strategy for the next decade or so.  And it was … Salesforce again.
But this time, he wasn’t just buying from sales. He bought directly from the CEO.
I asked how that worked and what happened.
“Why did you buy direct?” I asked?
He said: “Because we wanted someone who would take our social contract seriously.”
That really stood out as a phrase.
“What do you mean by ‘social contract’,” I asked?
“You know, like the Founding Fathers signed a social compact” he replied. “They took an oath to uphold certain principles and standards when they governed America. We want vendors that will sign up to those same contracts. It’s not enough to have your logo and be certified or whatever. Those are table stakes now. But we need folks that will commit to making sure everything works right, no matter what happens.”
Wow.
This is something almost none of us think about these days. We’re all thinking about PLG (product-led growth) and AI agents and more. But there are still many customers where signing up for a serious social contract matters.
If nothing else, if you sell to enterprises, make sure you understand what that means. Make sure every stakeholder has skin in the game, and everyone knows it.
It can lead to real loyalty over decades.
And even to being able to close deals where you aren’t the only vendor. Or even the cheapest.
Sometimes, having fewer features is actually a competitive advantage in larger enterprise deals.

I've been doing this for a while, and I have learned one thing that is pretty interesting. And it's counterintuitive.
I find as you go from $1 million in ARR up to about $10 million or so in ARR, things get more efficient, but they don't really change all that much. It gets harder every year at least because there are more people to manage and there are more stakeholders, but fundamentally, it doesn't change that much.
But what does change dramatically after $10 million in ARR is how customers buy software. They start buying enterprise software very differently than before. Now, you're probably thinking, "Well, we just sell on price." No, no, no. That's not true at all. There are two things going on here that make me want to scream when I see sales reps selling to enterprises who haven't sold to them before. First, buyers will give your product far more leeway if they trust you. That sounds obvious, right? Well, let me tell you what most startups do wrong with their marketing. Most startups think they can be trusted by talking about how great they are. What they need to do is talk about how much money they'll save you, which you might not even know until you use their product. This is the mistake that SaaS companies often make. We try to position ourselves as a solution for pain points we may not even understand yet. Let me tell you something that has worked incredibly well. We've done some case studies where we went out and interviewed our prospects ahead of time, found out exactly what was bugging them, then put those problems into a white paper that talked about the problem, the issue, and why they were losing money due to this particular problem. Then we sent it over to the prospect ahead of time and said, "Hey, check this out and call us back."
What happens? Every single time—every single time—the buyer calls back within minutes.

So we’ve done deep dives on many Cloud leaders over the years.  But one I’d like to do more often is Monday.com.
Monday.com has built something truly great — an incredible platform that’s not only highly usable and loved by its customers (and employees), but also incredibly efficient and profitable as well.  It’s now approaching $500m in ARR growing 30%+ … with 23% operating margins!
And it’s worth almost $10 Billion (!).
Let’s dig in:
#1.  Almost Half Their Revenue Comes From Outside North America
A reminder that SaaS can work just fine without being U.S.-centric if you want to go global early.
#2.  A Very Capital Efficient Engine.  And Profitable.
This may be our #1 learning here.  With 1000s of SMB customers paying mostly monthly, it doesn’t take much capital to acquire them.  So while most public software companies are trading at 7x-8x revenue or higher, Monday.com trades at just 6x revenues.  Less than half of HubSpot.
Also importantly, they don’t need massive sales teams to close their deals.  In fact, their CRO told me he thinks his team is already too big.  The self-service motion works really well for Monday.
It’s pretty efficient.  They spend less than 25 cents per dollar on sales & marketing, compared to 35%-40% for other high growth SaaS leaders.
#3.  $300k Customers Growing Quickly.  But Smaller Ones Are Even Faster
We saw this recently with Asana as well, but again, it shows how critical your smallest customers are in driving growth.  Yes, $250k ACV customers are key to Monday’s engine.  But so far, even smaller ones have grown faster.  That makes sense given how easy Monday is to use.

So we've talked quite a bit on SaaStr about Monday and its CEO Eran Zinman since it was one of our first public company portfolio investments.
And today it's crossing almost $600m ARR.  And growing a stunning 40% at that scale.
Wow.

But what can we learn?  How do they still grow so fast at almost $600m in ARR?

A few interesting learnings:

#1.  50% of their customers pay less than $10k a year
.  This is pretty common for many SMB leaders like Shopify, ZoomInfo, etc., but perhaps not as much for some others like HubSpot or Squarespace that are more enterprise-focused in their customer base.  A reminder to go long with your smallest customers if you want them to be happy, even if they often churn faster.
Monday has 230,000+ customers paying an average of just over $2,500 each.
That's pretty impressive efficiency at this scale!

#2. 30% of revenue outside U.S.
Another good lesson to see Monday doing well globally.  It does have offices around the world, but it doesn't seem to focus there per se.  Many folks don't realize how global Monday actually is -- and I think they'll benefit here going forward.  The world is moving to work together again post-Covid, at least partially.
This is another good reminder to Go Global Early if possible.

#3.  120% NRR overall; 140% from larger accounts.
We saw similar results with Smartsheet when it IPO'd (which was acquired by Adobe) and also with Asana which got to 100% NRR for a while before growth slowed.  But Monday shows us that high NRR isn't dead!   While most SaaS companies struggle to get above 110%-120% NRR these days, Monday gets there by focusing on adding value to its existing customer base.  So far at least, it hasn't been enough to propel it past 40% growth at $600m in ARR.  But maybe it will help fuel the next level of growth.

Dear SaaStr: What’s The Best Way To Stand Out In A Job Interview?
A few ideas:
Share your top mistakes. We all make them. But sharing what you’ve learned from is great.
Talk about how you are truly better than 90%+ of others that have done this job before
. This will always work if you can be honest and self-aware enough to do it. It doesn’t matter who you worked for or at — everyone has their flaws.
Ask for an hour with whomever will hire you. And ask to talk to some of those already on the team doing the job
. If they don’t want to give you time with someone other than the CEO / VP … well, run. Don’t take the role.
Be yourself. You’ll stand out as being different
. Be respectful but authentic. Share stories about when you succeeded, and even more importantly, share stories about when you failed. Everyone loves hearing about real failures (and success) 🙂
Show up early
. Show up to every interview looking sharp and rested. Send over notes ahead of time, etc.
Make sure there’s no reason not to hire you
. Make sure there isn’t any negative information out there. Especially today, where most recruiters use AI screening tools.
The best candidates don’t need to do much extra here. They just show up prepared and ready to rock.

answer:
So we've talked for years on this series and I think it's time to bring back one of our most popular sessions. It was great when Samantha Madhosingh was CRO at ZoomInfo and then later joined us as Chief Operating Officer here at SaaStr. And she did an incredible session with me that we're going to go through today called "How To Truly Stand Out In Every Interview". So first let's take a look what happens today in interviews.
[00:01:18]
The average interviewer spends five minutes reviewing your resume before they start the interview. Five minutes. You know, there are some exceptions out there where folks like to do reference checks or have other people review resumes ahead of time, but generally speaking, you're not getting any additional help unless you're interviewing at Salesforce or somewhere else. But even if you are, those folks aren't reading your resume until after they finish talking to you. There is no one doing research on who you are or how you can solve their problems beforehand. And I'm so tired of hearing folks say, "Oh, my recruiter told them all about me." That does happen sometimes. If you have a very high level recruiter that really knows you well, sometimes they'll prep the interviewer. Sometimes they will set up a meeting between the CEO and the candidate before the interview. But don't rely on that too much. Because more often than not, the person conducting your interview hasn't heard anything good about you yet. They haven't read your resume. The best way to stand out in every job interview is to immediately answer the question: "What makes you the right fit for this role?"
[00:02:29]
That's it. Now I hear so many candidates get nervous during interviews. Their brain goes blank. They sweat. And the last thing they want to do is talk about why they'd be perfect for the role. They would rather tell the story again of why they quit their last company. Why they failed, how they were fired, or how they had to leave because the VCs wouldn't give them enough money. I mean, I get it. We all want to share these stories. But the worst way to make yourself memorable is by telling someone a story they already know. Your job is to educate the interviewer on why you're the right fit for the position. Here's how to do it. Before you show up to an interview, whether it's in-person or virtual, find out everything you possibly can about the company. Go to Glassdoor.com. Read reviews from employees. Look at the website. Find out who works there and see if anyone shares similar experiences online. This isn't just about learning facts. It's about understanding the culture. What motivates the team? What keeps them coming into work every day? Be prepared to speak specifically about how your skills align with the company's needs. Don't generalize.

In addition to teaching at HBS, he has also taught at Northeastern University and Babson College. ______

There are winners in the marketplace who keep winning, but those that don’t need to evolve very quickly. If you look at the data points, many startups aren’t really innovating anymore.

Sales cycles stretching even longer (even at Salesforce)

You Can’t Cut Your Way To Growth. What Every Founder Should Know About Hiring Right Now. | SaaStr
Even worse … even when deals do happen, closing rates remain stuck around 10%-12%
. Everyone talks about how hard it is these days to “get a meeting”. answer:
Q:  I’m an SMB SaaS company with relatively high churn and low net retention. I’ve been growing my revenue at a good rate, but if your Net Retention Rate (NRR) is below 100% … you’ll run out of room.
You will grow faster than average for a while — because there are so many more customers you can get. But eventually, it all runs out. And then growth decelerates dramatically. It’s hard enough to hit $10m ARR with even a mediocre product. You may well be able to do better with say a 120%-130% NRR … if you have something great. Even without being truly enterprise-grade. But if your NRR is too low, you won’t really make it past that first initial phase. So what should we do?
A few thoughts:
First, don’t overindex on “churn reduction” as your top goal. That sounds easy, but it isn’t. The best way to reduce churn is to increase net negative churn. Get them spending more money, not just keeping their credit cards in their wallets. This means focusing most of your energy here after $1m-$2m ARR or so, when you have enough data to see which accounts you can upsell into. Second, stop blaming everyone else for your problems
. Your competitors often aren’t doing much better. Third, focus on increasing ACV per customer. A bit more here:
How To Increase Your Average Customer Value Per Account | SaaStr
Fourth, find some budget to invest back in sales & marketing
. At least 20% of any incremental cash flow. Yes, this means less investment in engineering. Maybe even zero new features until you’ve grown enough to justify a larger team. Fifth, push through it. In fact, once you’ve crossed Initial Traction ($5-8m+ ARR), lean in even harder now. Every dollar invested will pay off. Sixth, challenge yourself to improve NRR by X%. Not by going from -12% to +6%, but go from -11% to -9%, for example. Or maybe from 85% to 90%.

Dear SaaStr: How long does it take to deploy an AI SDR?
It can be done today.  We did it last year.
The key is you have to start with what already works, and build off that.  You probably already use HubSpot or Salesforce for your CRM, Marketo (or something similar) as your marketing automation platform, etc.  So you don’t need to buy anything new — at least not right away.  At least not if you are starting small.
But you do need someone on your team to manage it every day, especially during the first few months. The agent won't magically work without training.
Here's our simple 5-step plan:
Step 1: Pick One Platform
You can try different ones, but we started with Qualified
because they've been doing this longer than anyone else and their product has been more mature from Day 0. That doesn't mean it wasn't still a lot of work.
Step 2: Start Small—One Use Case
Pick one thing you want to automate. For us, it was outbound follow-up emails to prospects who'd visited our website but hadn't converted yet. We wanted to send them a series of automated emails instead of waiting weeks for human sales reps to respond.
Step 3: Connect Everything to Your Data Source
Link it to your CRM. Link it to whatever data source you're using. If you're using Salesforce, HubSpot, whatever—it needs to connect. Otherwise, the AI Agent will just make stuff up, which is terrible.
Step 4: Train the Agent Every Single Day
This is crucial. Every morning before breakfast, spend time with your AI Agent. Go through the leads it generated overnight. Review everything. Make sure nothing went wrong. Tell it why things were good or bad. This daily investment is non-negotiable.

Dear SaaStr: Should I Use an AI SDR Before You Have a Working Human SDR Motion?
I’d say yes.
First, most humans don’t want to do this work.  They can’t or won’t do it well enough anyway:
They’ll only call and email their favorite prospects and accounts they already know;
Most reps just send generic emails and never really research the prospect before sending them;
Few truly learn how best to sequence follow-up cadences for different types of leads; and
Even fewer will constantly improve and refine the scripts and messaging over time.
AI is always improving its approach here, and doesn’t get tired, frustrated, etc.  It’s always working on improving what it does, getting better at every interaction, and learning more about your product and ICP every day.
So if you have any leads that aren’t great fit for a human rep — but are still worth following up with — use an AI agent instead.
It’s almost always better than nothing.  And much less expensive than trying to train someone who isn’t going to do it right.
And importantly, there’s no reason not to run both in parallel until you see which performs better.
There’s zero cost in running both an AI and a human SDR in parallel for now.  There may be some marginal overlap (the AI might reach out to folks your human SDRs also call), but overall the volume should be manageable.
The bottom line is, don’t let perfect being the enemy of good.  The vast majority of start-ups don’t even try outbound sales because it seems too hard.  But they miss the chance to drive in some qualified leads and revenue from the contacts in the database.
If you’ve got something that works with AI … roll it out today.  Then later add humans into the mix once you need more personalization, more nuance, and/or when you have a team big enough to make it all scale.
But don’t wait for perfection.

Dear SaaStr: How do you know if you are ready for venture capital?
There is no perfect test, but here’s how I think about it:
First,
if you aren’t growing quickly enough (say 50%-80%), or have too low NPS / churn, etc. — don’t bother.
It will be hard to get funded then and/or at a reasonable price.  There just won’t be much interest from VCs.
Second, there really needs to be something special, one way or another.  This could be your team, an incredible market pull, viral growth … or even just being super early.  Or a great brand that customers love.
Third, you need to understand what stage you are at.  Most investors want to see you’ve crossed Initial Traction ($1-$2m ARR) and are on track to cross Initial Scale ($10m+ ARR).  If not, they’ll often pass unless there is real magic going on somewhere else.  More
here
.
Fourth, if you can show the potential for a $100b+ exit down the road — that can sometimes overcome things like “only” 40% monthly growth.  You gotta talk up these numbers, because otherwise, folks may worry they are unrealistic.
Fifth, sometimes it takes time to find someone that believes in you.  Just keep trying.

And finally, maybe most importantly, ask around.  Talk to other founders, especially ones that have raised a round recently.  They should have some good ideas on where you stand and why.  And also, ask them directly who they’d fund today, and why.  That will help clarify a lot of issues as well.
I’m proud to say our first seed investor was a Y Combinator partner, which helped us raise more money later.  It’s OK if you haven’t done this before, though.  The best VCs usually already know each other, so it works out.

So one of the most common objections I hear from traditional SaaS execs to going deeper with AI is that customers won’t trust an AI.
That it’s too new, and they don’t want their data touched by anything not run by humans.  Or at least, more than just code reviewed by humans.
And there may be some truth here — for now.
But already:
I recently bought a house through ChatGPT / Claude directly on my own phone
.  It worked like magic, without any human involved.   No agent.   Just me, Claude, and our AI real estate buying system.  And we did it all ourselves … except for when Claude told us to hire a lawyer 😉
I also had my first meeting this week with an AI Agent selling me a product I’ve never used before.  That would have been almost impossible pre-AI.  Because no human could possibly know enough to sell me something I’d never heard of before.
Now you can see these two examples aren’t exactly enterprise software use cases 🙂
But they are the future.
The old model was based on scarcity. A sales rep knew everything because they were the only one who could help. An FDE knew your deployment because they’d set it up for you once. Support agents knew your issue history because someone else typed it into the CRM.
AI flips this on its head. We’re seeing companies where revenue per agent has skyrocketed even as customer counts explode—because each agent becomes infinitely scalable while maintaining deep, personalized knowledge of every single customer interaction.
This isn’t science fiction anymore.
Already today,
we’re seeing customers buy complex products (like a home) entirely autonomously using AI
and having meaningful interactions with AI Agents for products they’ve never tried before.
What does that mean for B2B?
It means the question shouldn’t be whether buyers will trust AI.

It works well when you train it properly:

But here’s what happened with our new AI SDR agent over the holidays (we learned this lesson again):
The vendor told us to just “train it” before they’d turn it live. So we did.  We trained it.  And then went off for vacation.

Outdated Training Data Drift
:
Our training dataset became stale while we weren’t actively checking outputs against real-time market conditions and prospect feedback patterns. Without fresh validation, responses started sounding robotic and disconnected from current market realities.
Edge Case Explosion
:
Without daily human oversight, edge case handling broke down completely. For example, the agent stopped knowing how to handle objections effectively or adapt to new sales scenarios that hadn’t been documented in historical training data.
Training Dataset Corruption
:
Someone accidentally deleted critical training materials while trying to optimize performance metrics, forcing us to rebuild entire segments of the model.

And I have to tell you something that's happened three times now at SaaStr. Three different AI agents. Two were our own internal tools we built ourselves. One was from a leading vendor.
All three failed catastrophically. All three went off rails. And all three we didn't even know until they'd already gone down. And why? Because when you train an AI agent, there are two phases. Phase one is training it on your data. That works great. It's like magic.

I mean, think about it. When your AI agent gives bad advice, it's not just your company that suffers. If your potential customer buys a product based on false information provided by your AI agent, then guess who takes the hit?

AI adoption in sales remains shockingly low despite being available for over two years. Only 39% of sellers have ever tried an AI tool, while 42% haven’t deployed any agents at all. Meanwhile, almost half of reps continue doing things exactly as before rather than adopting best practices, and nearly three-quarters say their current tools need improvement. The numbers reveal a culture stuck in traditional methods despite having access to modern capabilities. For B2B founders, this creates both opportunity and urgency—they can either lead from the front with innovative approaches or risk getting left behind by competitors who embrace transformation faster.

First, ask yourself if you can truly win them back. Sometimes it’s better just to let them go.

Let them have their data

Make sure someone always follows up ASAP when a customer threatens to leave. And ideally, before they pay their last penny. When they don't get a follow-up call, and/or aren't heard, they almost always assume the product isn't worth it anymore. But maybe it still is. Maybe a few months down the road, they'd come back. Don't let those customers go without trying every trick in the book.

Dear SaaStr: Is It Bad To Leave a Start-Up That's Not Going Very Well?
It’s not always bad. But if you leave too early, your career often suffers.
First, think about why you want to leave:
Are you burnt out from working long hours with no end in sight?
Do you feel undervalued or overworked without adequate compensation?
Is there no clear path for growth or advancement within the company?
If these are your reasons, it might be time to move on. Staying at a struggling startup can take a toll on both your mental and physical health. You deserve better.
But ask yourself one more question before making any decisions:

What do I need to learn here that will help me succeed elsewhere?
If you’re leaving because you don’t see success ahead, but you haven’t learned everything you could, you might regret it later.

A few things to consider:

How many startups have you worked at?
Have you experienced the full cycle—from idea generation through scale-up and IPO (if possible)?
Can you point to specific lessons—whether they were successes or failures—that helped shape who you are as an entrepreneur today?

Most importantly: what skills would you bring to your next role that you wouldn't otherwise have gained by staying through this challenging period?
Sometimes the best learning comes from experiencing failure firsthand. The companies we remember most aren't those that succeeded immediately; they're those that pushed through adversity to become something remarkable.

So while leaving may seem like the easy way out, it isn't always the right choice. Sometimes the hardest choices are the ones where you stay, fight, and learn.
And maybe … maybe find a new CEO.
I joined a start-up when it had just $20k MRR growing slowly. It was tough, but we got to $2m ARR growing 100% YoY. Then the cofounder left to go back to his old job. I tried to carry it further, but ultimately couldn't make it work.
Yes, I'd made some mistakes, and our customers didn't love us enough, etc. But I've never looked back and said I should have quit sooner. In fact, I wish I'd hired someone to help run it instead!
In contrast, my second start-up took off faster than expected. We hit $1M ARR in less than 12 months. And then... we lost almost all our leads overnight due to a big change in how Google works. So far, so good — we went down from $200k+ MRR to $0 overnight. Still, still doing fine. We're at $500k-$600k MRR now.
The thing is, I really wanted to quit after the first month or two, when things slowed down. But my co-founder talked me into it. My advice to you would be to try harder. Push even harder, and push longer. Maybe get another VP, hire a great sales team, improve the product, figure out how to market better, whatever it takes.

So I’ve been thinking for some time, since we launched SaaStr.ai with over 20 AI agents … that there’s this paradox out there.
On one hand, you can do so much more today than before when we had humans doing it all ourselves.  And on the other hand …
We’re already working harder than ever before.  Not just me and my team — but everyone at scale.  Everyone managing larger teams now is also working far, far harder than even 24 months ago:
The productivity gains are real
But they don’t translate to less work
They actually lead to more work, or certainly different types of work
Why This Happens: The “Cowan Effect”
Let’s start with what economist Roy Cowan identified back in 1970s Britain. He found something remarkable among factory workers:
Productivity increases didn’t reduce working hours—they increased them
When workers became more efficient, their employers simply gave them more tasks to complete
Rather than enjoying leisure time from automation, people ended up working longer, producing more, and often earning higher wages
This isn’t about greed—this is economics. When your marginal cost goes down (in this case, labor), your willingness to take on additional output goes up. It becomes cheaper to expand production lines. To ship more product. To run more shifts. In our context, here’s how it plays out:
AI makes every task faster and better. That means we can handle:
More speaking engagements
More content creation
Deeper analysis of sponsors and speakers
Better match-making between founders and investors
And because we have these capabilities, we’re using them to produce MORE output—not less
Same thing with sales and GTM. We deployed an AI agent to manage outbound follow-ups and qualification calls. Instead of running 2-300 emails per week manually, we now send thousands automatically.

So I’ve been investing and advising on quite a few hot AI startups these days, from $20m ARR to hundreds of millions.
One thing that has become clear is there are two sales strategies:
Strategy #1: “High Velocity” — Hire as Many AEs as Possible ASAP
The goal here is to hit the number for this year, no matter what it takes.  As soon as you have even 10-15 customers paying decent amounts per month, you hire enough AEs so they can close as many deals as possible … quickly.  This often means hiring 5 or more AEs before you really know if they work.
This approach makes sense when:
You’re already seeing strong demand pull from prospects
You need to close X million dollars by end-of-year to prove traction
Your CRO/CEO wants to make quota (and fast)
You’re in hypergrowth mode where every dollar matters immediately
But here’s the catch—and most founders miss it:
These new hires will be mostly useless until you give them something to sell. If your product isn’t battle-tested, doesn’t have clear use cases, or lacks real ROI data, those 20 reps won’t magically create pipeline out of thin air. They’ll just spend their time talking to prospects who aren’t ready to buy yet—or worse, get frustrated trying to demo features that don’t actually work.
And then Strategy #2: Slow & Steady—Build Depth Before Scale
Hire only when you truly believe the rep will succeed. Wait until you have a repeatable process, proven use cases, solid customer success stories, and actual ROI metrics to back up your pitch. Then hire one great AE who knows how to sell it, not 20 mediocre ones hoping for luck.
This approach works best when:
Your product needs serious maturation
Prospects want proof points before committing
You’re still refining your go-to-market motion
Customer success stories take months, not weeks, to develop
The Problem With High Velocity Hiring Without Product Readiness
I see too many early-stage companies following strategy #1 without realizing they’re setting themselves up for disaster down the line. Here’s what happens:
Month 1–3: Reps struggle because the product isn’t reliable or scalable. They lose credibility with prospects who hear contradictory things about capabilities.

We’ve talked on SaaStr many times how to manage cash.  But one thing I haven’t done enough is talk about how to avoid running out.
Yes, you can run a model and see when your runway ends. And maybe even build a zero-cash plan for next year.  But what if … you just don’t have time?  What if it’s too late?
Let me share my learnings here:
First,
never let your burn rate exceed twice your monthly revenue
.  This isn’t a rule per se, but it works well for most startups that raise some VC capital at least.  If you’re burning more than twice your last month’s MRR / ARR — then something has gone wrong.  You aren’t growing fast enough.  The sales team isn’t performing well enough.  Your CTO doesn’t know how to scale the product.  Something.
Because that means you’ll be running out of money in less than a year.
Second,
if you are worried you might run out of money before Year Two or so, never spend anything without talking to your co-founder first
.  Even if they don’t want to hear it.
In fact, make sure this is part of any investment round pitch deck discussion.  It should always come up.  “If we do worse than X, our cash will run out.”  Or “we expect $Xm ARR by Y months after funding.”
The point is you need to discuss it.  Every single week.  A few ideas:
Don’t hire anyone with no equity until you have real traction.
Do not hire an unaffordable VP.
Never take a bonus or salary increase unless you have plenty of cash.
Never add another layer of management unless you really have the cash to pay them all.
I remember the exact day I spent everything — Day -1.  We’d had a huge blow-out party celebrating hitting $20k MRR (the final number was $18k).  Then the next day, I looked at the books, saw we were over budget, and knew we couldn’t afford to keep going.  I quit.
But there are things you can do to save money each month, every month.  If you start now, you won’t ever get close to running out of money again.  At least, not from overspending.
And importantly, having these conversations regularly makes it much easier to find new ways to conserve cash.  Because everyone is thinking about it all the time.

I’ve been saying this for months now, but it bears repeating:
SaaS isn’t dead.
It’s still growing faster than most other categories. It’s still the largest software market in history. The majority of public companies are still seeing acceleration from AI. And buyers still want products that make their lives easier and more efficient.
But here’s what I can tell you with absolute certainty after running 11+ years of SaaStr content, investing in hundreds of B2B companies, and watching thousands of pitches:
The playbook has fundamentally changed. Not just a little bit — completely and irreversibly. What Worked Before (and Still Does)
Let me be clear: if your product was great before March 2024, it should work today. Great products always win. If you had strong unit economics, good retention, and happy customers — none of that changes. Customers will still pay for things they love. They’ll still renew contracts where they’re getting real value. The fundamentals haven’t broken.
What Has Broken (And Why)
Here’s what ISN’T working anymore, even if your core product works fine:
#1. “We Have More Features Than Anybody Else”
This used to be table stakes. A decade ago, adding features was how you won competitive battles. Every sales call sounded like “Well actually, our version does THIS, which yours doesn’t.”
Customers would nod politely and take notes because having options made them feel empowered. Today? No one cares. Everyone now expects you to have all the features. In fact, being feature-poor has become an advantage in many cases.

SaaS isn't dead. In fact, we're spending more on software today than ever before.
$1 trillion annually. Up from $600 billion five years ago.

That's why Microsoft stock was up 35% over the past twelve months while everyone else got hammered.
And when I look across my portfolio companies, none of them are struggling because they sold too much software. They're struggling because they didn't sell enough software that matters anymore. So let's take a deep dive on what's really happening. Why AI hype doesn't equal revenue growth.
